posts:
Before judging a support team's performance, look at the workload it's handling.

A rise in ticket volume might reflect a product issue, seasonal demand, or increased customer activity. The total alone won't explain what's happening.

Try breaking ticket volume down by channel, category, and time period. Those comparisons can help you understand whether the team is facing a general increase in demand or a specific problem that needs attention.

posts:
Monthly recurring revenue gives you a useful starting point for understanding a subscription business.

Track MRR over time to see whether the recurring revenue base is expanding, contracting, or staying relatively stable. Then look at the size and consistency of those changes rather than focusing only on the latest total.

Try comparing the last six months of MRR. Is growth accelerating, slowing, or becoming more unpredictable?

A business can report strong profits and still face pressure on its cash flow.

Revenue and profitability help explain financial performance, but they don't always show when money will actually arrive or leave the business. Understanding both perspectives matters when planning ahead.

My Financial Performance & Cash Flow Power BI Kit brings these views together: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4595413257/power-bi-financial-dashboard-template-13

media.alt: Preview of the Financial Performance & Cash Flow Power BI Dashboard Kit

posts:
Revenue is growing, margins are holding steady, and cash balances are declining. What does that tell you?

Each measure describes a different part of financial performance. The combination may point toward working capital needs, payment timing, or other factors worth investigating.

Try reviewing revenue, profitability, and cash trends side by side for the same reporting periods. Where do the trends agree, and where do they tell different stories?

Your sales dashboard might only be telling half the story.

Revenue is important, but understanding which products drive sales, how transactions are recorded, and what the business is purchasing adds valuable context. Those details help build a fuller picture of commercial performance.

My Sales Performance & Commercial Operations Power BI Kit brings these views together: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4595438858/power-bi-sales-dashboard-template-sales

posts:
Revenue is a useful starting point for sales reporting, but it becomes more meaningful alongside other measures.

Order counts, units sold, and average order value help explain how sales activity is developing. Looking at these metrics over time can reveal changes that a single revenue figure might miss.

Try comparing revenue growth with changes in order volume and average order value. Is growth coming from more orders, larger orders, or a combination of both?

Your sales numbers only tell half the story.

Revenue shows what a business generated, but understanding employee contributions, product performance, and location results adds important context. Those details can help explain what's happening across the organization.

My Workforce Performance & Sales Activity Power BI Kit brings these perspectives together in three editable dashboard pages: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4595444828/power-bi-sales-performance-dashboard

posts:
A revenue total becomes more useful when you can see what contributed to it.

Sales targets, gross profit, and employee activity provide additional perspectives on performance. Reviewing these measures together helps you understand results beyond the headline number.

Try looking at your latest sales report and asking three questions: How are we performing against targets? What does profitability look like? Where are employees contributing most?

Your field team is busy. But is it performing?

A full schedule can show how much work was assigned or completed, but it doesn't explain productivity, service quality, or repeat visits. Those details matter when you're trying to understand how the team is actually doing.

My Field Team Performance Power BI Kit includes four editable dashboards for exploring these questions: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4595448076/power-bi-field-team-performance

posts:
Before digging into individual field jobs, it helps to understand the bigger picture.

Completion rates, productivity, repeat work, and performance against targets can reveal different aspects of how a field operation is running. Reviewing them together gives managers a more useful starting point.

Try choosing four measures for a weekly field team overview. Make sure they cover output, efficiency, quality, and progress toward expectations.

A full business development pipeline doesn't always mean a healthy pipeline.

A large total opportunity value can look encouraging, but it doesn't explain how likely those opportunities are to close or how much business has actually been won. The details behind the total matter.

My Business Development Performance Power BI Kit helps explore that broader picture: https://garrettsdevdesk.etsy.com/listing/4595453904/power-bi-business-development-dashboard

media.alt: Preview of the Business Development Performance Power BI Dashboard Kit

posts:
Pipeline value becomes more useful when you add context.

Total opportunity value shows the size of potential business. Probability-weighted value provides another perspective, while won business shows what has actually converted. Looking at all three can help prevent overly optimistic interpretations.

Try putting total pipeline, weighted pipeline, and won value side by side in your next review. Notice how each changes the conversation.
